claim: Dopamine axons are the only axons known to grow during adolescence.
source: Dopamine axons are the only axons known to grow during adolescence.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript itself, but is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Dopamine axons reach the cortex through a transient gradient of Netrin-1-expressing cells in mice.
source: We demonstrate in mice (Mus musculus) that dopamine axons reach the cortex through a transient gradient of Netrin-1-expressing cells – disrupting this gradient reroutes axons away from their target.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing Netrin-1 gradient (Figure 1H, I) and viral knockdown experiments (Figure 1L).

claim: Disrupting the Netrin-1 gradient reroutes dopamine axons away from their target.
source: We demonstrate in mice (Mus musculus) that dopamine axons reach the cortex through a transient gradient of Netrin-1-expressing cells – disrupting this gradient reroutes axons away from their target.
evidence: Supported by viral knockdown experiment showing reduced TH+ varicosity density in infralimbic cortex (Figure 1L).

claim: Mesocortical dopamine development can be regulated by daylength in Siberian hamsters.
source: Using a seasonal model (Siberian hamsters; Phodopus sungorus) we find that mesocortical dopamine development can be regulated by a natural environmental cue (daylength) in a sexually dimorphic manner – delayed in males, but advanced in females.
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification of dopamine innervation in hamsters under different photoperiods (Figures 3C, D and 4C, D, E).

claim: Daylength regulation of mesocortical dopamine development is sexually dimorphic, delayed in males but advanced in females.
source: Using a seasonal model (Siberian hamsters; Phodopus sungorus) we find that mesocortical dopamine development can be regulated by a natural environmental cue (daylength) in a sexually dimorphic manner – delayed in males, but advanced in females.
evidence: Supported by comparison of male (Figure 3D) and female (Figure 4D, E) hamster data showing opposite effects of winter photoperiod.

claim: The timings of dopamine axon growth and UNC5C expression are always phase-locked.
source: The timings of dopamine axon growth and UNC5C expression are always phase-locked.
evidence: Supported by parallel timing of UNC5C expression and dopamine innervation across multiple conditions in mice and hamsters (Figures 2, 3, 4).

claim: The prefrontal cortex is still establishing connections during adolescence.
source: The prefrontal cortex, the brain region responsible for our most complex cognitive functions, is still establishing connections during this time (Gogtay et al., 2004; Petanjek et al., 2011; Sowell et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The trajectory of prefrontal cortex development in adolescence determines vulnerability or resilience to adolescent-onset psychiatric diseases.
source: The trajectory of prefrontal cortex development in adolescence determines the vulnerability or resilience of individuals to adolescent-onset psychiatric diseases (Fuhrmann et al., 2015; Keshavan et al., 2014; Kessler et al., 2007; Kessler et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The onset of adolescence traditionally coincides with puberty.
source: Traditionally, the onset of adolescence is thought to coincide with puberty (Hollenstein and Lougheed, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The age of pubertal onset has been advancing throughout the 19th, 20th, and 21st centuries in humans.
source: In humans, the age of pubertal onset has been advancing throughout the 19th, 20th, and 21st centuries, and environmental influences, such as nutrition, can pathologically alter the age of puberty (Wolf and Long, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Environmental influences such as nutrition can pathologically alter the age of puberty.
source: In humans, the age of pubertal onset has been advancing throughout the 19th, 20th, and 21st centuries, and environmental influences, such as nutrition, can pathologically alter the age of puberty (Wolf and Long, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Dopamine innervation to the prefrontal cortex increases substantially across adolescence.
source: Dopamine innervation to the prefrontal cortex increases substantially across adolescence, and psychopathologies of adolescent origin prominently feature dopamine dysfunction.
evidence: Supported by data in the manuscript (Figures 1E, 3C, 4C) and citations to previous literature.

claim: Psychopathologies of adolescent origin prominently feature dopamine dysfunction.
source: Dopamine innervation to the prefrontal cortex increases substantially across adolescence, and psychopathologies of adolescent origin prominently feature dopamine dysfunction.
evidence: Supported by general scientific knowledge and context.

claim: Protracted dopamine innervation is a key neural process underlying cognitive and behavioural changes that characterise adolescence.
source: Evidence continues to emerge that protracted dopamine innervation is a key neural process underlying the cognitive and behavioural changes that characterise adolescence (Larsen and Luna, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: At the onset of adolescence, both mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine axons innervate the nucleus accumbens in rodents.
source: At the onset of adolescence, both mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine axons innervate the nucleus accumbens in rodents, but the mesocortical axons leave the accumbens and grow toward the prefrontal cortex during adolescence and early adulthood (Hoops et al., 2018; Reynolds et al., 2018; Reynolds et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mesocortical dopamine axons leave the nucleus accumbens and grow toward the prefrontal cortex during adolescence and early adulthood.
source: At the onset of adolescence, both mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine axons innervate the nucleus accumbens in rodents, but the mesocortical axons leave the accumbens and grow toward the prefrontal cortex during adolescence and early adulthood (Hoops et al., 2018; Reynolds et al., 2018; Reynolds et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature and data in the manuscript.

claim: Dopamine axon growth from one brain region to another during adolescence is the only known case of such late developmental axon growth.
source: This is the only known case of axons growing from one brain region to another so late during development (Reynolds and Flores, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Environmental insults during adolescence alter the extent and organisation of dopamine innervation in the prefrontal cortex in mice.
source: Environmental insults during adolescence (e.g. drug abuse) alter the extent and organisation of dopamine innervation in the prefrontal cortex, leading to behavioural and cognitive changes in mice throughout adulthood (Drzewiecki and Juraska, 2020; Hoops and Flores, 2017; Reynolds and Flores, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Alterations in dopamine innervation during adolescence lead to behavioural and cognitive changes in mice throughout adulthood.
source: Environmental insults during adolescence (e.g. drug abuse) alter the extent and organisation of dopamine innervation in the prefrontal cortex, leading to behavioural and cognitive changes in mice throughout adulthood (Drzewiecki and Juraska, 2020; Hoops and Flores, 2017; Reynolds and Flores, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cognitive control develops in parallel with dopamine innervation to the cortex in adolescence.
source: These changes often involve cognitive control, a prefrontal function that develops in parallel with dopamine innervation to the cortex in adolescence (Luna et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Disruption of dopamine innervation frequently results in 'immature' cognitive control persisting through adulthood.
source: Disruption of dopamine innervation frequently seems to result in 'immature' cognitive control persisting through adulthood (Reynolds and Flores, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Netrin-1 interaction with its receptor DCC determines which dopamine axons establish connections in the nucleus accumbens and which grow to the prefrontal cortex.
source: The guidance cue molecule Netrin-1, upon interacting with its receptor DCC, determines which dopamine axons establish connections in the nucleus accumbens and which ones leave this region to grow to the prefrontal cortex (Hoops and Flores, 2017; Reynolds and Flores, 2021; Reynolds et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dopamine axons medial to the nucleus accumbens occupy a distinct area and are oriented dorsally toward the cortex in adult mice.
source: We observed that dopamine axons medial to the nucleus accumbens occupy a distinct area and are oriented dorsally toward the cortex (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry images in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Individual dopamine fibres can be seen crossing the boundary of the nucleus accumbens shell and joining dorsally oriented axons.
source: Individual fibres can be seen crossing the boundary of the nucleus accumbens shell and joining these dorsally oriented axons (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry image in Figure 1C.

claim: The density of dopamine axons does not change between adolescence (21 days) and adulthood (75 days) in male and female mice.
source: We found, in both male and female mice, that the density of dopamine axons does not change between adolescence (21 days of age) and adulthood (75 days of age; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The width of the area that dopamine axons occupy increases between adolescence and adulthood in mice.
source: However, the width of the area that dopamine axons occupy does change, increasing between adolescence and adulthood (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The total number of dopamine axons passing through the area medial to the nucleus accumbens increases over adolescence.
source: These results indicate that the total number of dopamine axons passing through this area increases over adolescence and that dopamine axons grow to the medial prefrontal cortex via this route.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of constant density and increasing width measurements.

claim: Dopamine axons grow to the medial prefrontal cortex via the route medial to the nucleus accumbens.
source: These results indicate that the total number of dopamine axons passing through this area increases over adolescence and that dopamine axons grow to the medial prefrontal cortex via this route.
evidence: Inferred from anatomical observations and quantification data.

claim: In adolescent mice, there are more Netrin-1-positive cells along the dopamine axon pathway than medial to it.
source: We found that in adolescence there are more Netrin-1-positive neurons within the dopamine axon route than adjacent to it.
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Along the dopamine axon route in adolescent mice, the density of Netrin-1-positive cells increases toward the medial prefrontal cortex, forming a dorsoventral gradient.
source: Furthermore, along the axon route the density of Netrin-1-positive cells increases toward the medial prefrontal cortex, forming a dorsoventral gradient (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In adult mice, there remains a higher density of Netrin-1-positive cells along the dopamine route compared to the adjacent region, but the dorsoventral gradient is no longer present.
source: In adulthood, there remains a higher density of Netrin-1-positive cells along the dopamine route compared to the adjacent region, however the dorsoventral gradient is no longer present (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Silencing Netrin-1 in the dorsal peduncular cortex at the onset of adolescence does not alter dopamine terminal density in the lateral septum in adulthood.
source: Silencing Netrin-1 did not alter dopamine terminal density below the injection, in the lateral septum (Figure 1L).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Silencing Netrin-1 in the dorsal peduncular cortex at the onset of adolescence reduces dopamine terminal density in the infralimbic cortex in adulthood.
source: In the infralimbic cortex, which is the first prefrontal cortical region the axons reach after the injection site, terminal density was reduced in the Netrin-1 knockdown group compared to controls (Figure 1L).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Netrin-1 knockdown appears to erase the Netrin-1 path to the prefrontal cortex, resulting in dopamine axons failing to reach their correct innervation target.
source: The knockdown appears to erase the Netrin-1 path to the prefrontal cortex, resulting in dopamine axons failing to reach their correct innervation target.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing reduced innervation after Netrin-1 knockdown.

claim: Netrin-1 expressing cells 'pave the way' for dopamine axons growing to the medial prefrontal cortex.
source: Nonetheless, our results allow us to conclude that Netrin-1 expressing cells 'pave the way' for dopamine axons growing to the medial prefrontal cortex.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the gradient data and knockdown experiments.

claim: Dopamine input to the prefrontal cortex is a key factor in the transition from juvenile to adult behaviours that occurs in adolescence.
source: Dopamine input to the prefrontal cortex is a key factor in the transition from juvenile to adult behaviours that occurs in adolescence.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge and context from the manuscript.

claim: Inhibitory control matures in parallel with the innervation of dopamine axons to the prefrontal cortex in adolescence.
source: This test quantifies inhibitory control, which matures in parallel with the innervation of dopamine axons to the prefrontal cortex in adolescence (Casey et al., 2008; Klune et al., 2021; Luna et al., 2015; Paus, 2005; Reynolds and Flores, 2021; Spear, 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Inhibitory control is impaired in adolescent-onset disorders like depression and schizophrenia.
source: and it is impaired in adolescent-onset disorders like depression and schizophrenia (Catts et al., 2013; Clementz et al., 2016; McTeague et al., 2016; Millan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mice injected with Netrin-1 silencing virus show improved action impulsivity compared to controls, incurring significantly fewer commission errors across the Go/No-Go task.
source: Mice injected with the Netrin-1 knockdown virus show improved action impulsivity compared to controls; they incur significantly fewer commission errors across the Go/No-Go task.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: During the first days of Go/No-Go testing, the Netrin-1 knockdown group has fewer commission errors than the control group.
source: During the first days of Go/No-Go testing, both groups incur commission errors with high frequency, but the Netrin-1 knockdown group has fewer errors than the control group (t-test, t=5.18, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1O.

claim: The ED50 (inflection point) does not differ between Netrin-1 knockdown and control groups in the Go/No-Go task.
source: The ED50 – the inflection point in each sigmoidal curve – does not differ between groups, indicating that all mice improve their ability to inhibit their behaviour at around the same time (t-test, t=0.97, p=0.35).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1P.

claim: Mice microinfused with Netrin-1 knockdown virus incur substantially fewer commission errors in the last days of the Go/No-Go task compared to control mice.
source: Mice microinfused with the Netrin-1 knockdown virus incur substantially fewer commission errors in the last days of the Go/No-Go task compared to mice injected with the control virus (t-test, t=12.38, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1Q.

claim: The maturation of action impulsivity is sensitive to the organisation of the ventro-dorsal Netrin-1 path that guides mesocortical dopamine axon growth.
source: These behavioural results demonstrate that the maturation of action impulsivity is sensitive to the organisation of the ventro-dorsal Netrin-1 path that guides mesocortical dopamine axon growth.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the behavioral results following Netrin-1 knockdown.

claim: Deviations in the Netrin-1 route associate with striking changes in cognitive development characteristic of adolescence.
source: Deviations in this route associate with striking changes in the cognitive development that is characteristic of adolescence.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the behavioral results following Netrin-1 knockdown.

claim: Netrin-1 pathway deviation leads to improved action impulsivity, suggesting ectopic innervation of a forebrain region other than the medial prefrontal cortex.
source: In this case, the deviation leads to improved action impulsivity, suggesting that these dopamine axons may end up ectopically innervating a forebrain region other than the medial prefrontal cortex, enhancing cognitive control.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: Only a small subset of dopamine axons that reach the nucleus accumbens by early adolescence leave for the cortex; the vast majority stay in the accumbens throughout life.
source: However, only a small subset of the dopamine axons that have reached the nucleus accumbens by early adolescence leave; the vast majority stay and form connections in the accumbens throughout life (Reynolds et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The 'decision-making' process of whether dopamine axons 'stay' in the accumbens or 'go' to the cortex happens during a narrow developmental window at the onset of adolescence.
source: The 'decision-making' process of whether to 'stay' (in the accumbens) or 'go' (to the cortex via the Netrin-1 path) happens during a narrow developmental window at the onset of adolescence (Reynolds et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Dopamine neurons begin to express the repulsive Netrin-1 receptor UNC5C in adolescence, particularly when mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine projections segregate in the nucleus accumbens.
source: In adolescence, dopamine neurons begin to express the repulsive Netrin-1 receptor UNC5C, particularly when mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine projections segregate in the nucleus accumbens (Manitt et al., 2010; Reynolds et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dopamine axons in the prefrontal cortex do not express UNC5c, except in very rare cases.
source: In contrast, dopamine axons in the prefrontal cortex do not express UNC5c, except in very rare cases (Appendix 1 - Supplementary Analysis 4).
evidence: Supported by data in supplementary analysis.

claim: In adult male mice with Unc5c haploinsufficiency, there appears to be ectopic growth of mesolimbic dopamine axons to the prefrontal cortex.
source: In adult male mice with Unc5c haploinsufficiency, there appears to be ectopic growth of mesolimbic dopamine axons to the prefrontal cortex (Auger et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ectopic dopamine axon growth in Unc5c haploinsufficient mice is associated with alterations in prefrontal cortex-dependent behaviours.
source: This miswiring is associated with alterations in prefrontal cortex-dependent behaviours (Auger et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In male mice, there is little expression of UNC5C on dopamine axons in the nucleus accumbens at the onset of adolescence (21 days old).
source: In male mice, we found little expression of UNC5C on dopamine axons at the onset of adolescence (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry image in Figure 2A.

claim: In adult male mice, dopamine axons in the nucleus accumbens express UNC5C.
source: while we did find UNC5C expression on dopamine axons in adults (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry image in Figure 2B.

claim: In female mice at the onset of adolescence (21 days old), dopamine axons in the nucleus accumbens already express UNC5C.
source: Remarkably, when we assessed this in females, we found dopamine axons already expressing UNC5C in the nucleus accumbens at the onset of adolescence (Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry image in Figure 2D.

claim: In adult female mice, dopamine axons in the nucleus accumbens express UNC5C.
source: similar to adult females (Figure 2E)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry image in Figure 2E.

claim: The onset of UNC5C expression on dopamine axons in the nucleus accumbens is sexually dimorphic, with an earlier emergence in females.
source: indicating that the onset of UNC5C expression on dopamine axons in the nucleus accumbens is sexually dimorphic, with an earlier emergence in females.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of male and female mouse data.

claim: In pre-adolescent female mice (15 days old), there is little UNC5C expression on dopamine axons in the nucleus accumbens.
source: We examined the nucleus accumbens in pre-adolescent female mice and indeed found little UNC5C expression on dopamine axons (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry image in Figure 2C.

claim: The onset of UNC5C expression in mesocorticolimbic dopamine axons is peri-adolescent but occurs earlier in females than in males.
source: The onset of UNC5C expression in mesocorticolimbic dopamine axons is therefore peri-adolescent but occurs earlier in females than in males, consistent with the earlier emergence of adolescence in female rodents and the earlier onset of adolescence and puberty in humans (Wolf and Long, 2016).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the data and comparison to known developmental patterns.

claim: Differences in the precise timing of dopamine innervation to the PFC in adolescence have been suggested by findings in male and female rats.
source: Differences in the precise timing of dopamine innervation to the PFC in adolescence have been suggested by findings reported in male and female rats (Willing et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Siberian hamsters regulate many aspects of their behaviour and physiology to meet the changing environmental demands of seasonality.
source: Siberian hamsters (Phodopus sungorus) regulate many aspects of their behaviour and physiology to meet the changing environmental demands of seasonality (Paul et al., 2008; Stevenson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In winter, Siberian hamsters increase the thickness of their fur, exchange their brown summer coats for white winter ones, and undergo daily torpor to conserve energy.
source: In winter, they increase the thickness of their fur, exchange their brown summer coats for white winter ones, and undergo a daily torpor to conserve energy (Scherbarth and Steinlechner, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Adult Siberian hamsters suppress reproduction and juveniles delay puberty in winter.
source: In addition, adults suppress reproduction and juveniles delay puberty (Pévet, 1988; Yellon and Goldman, 1984), including developmental changes in gonadotropin releasing hormone neurons in the hypothalamus (Buchanan and Yellon, 1991; Heywood and Yellon, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Reproductive organ development is delayed as part of pubertal postponement in Siberian hamsters.
source: Reproductive organ development is delayed as part of pubertal postponement (Darrow et al., 1980; Ebling, 1994; Timonin et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Seasonal plasticity in Siberian hamsters is regulated by long or short periods of daylight.
source: This seasonal plasticity is regulated by long or short periods of daylight (Heldmaier and Steinlechner, 1981; Hoffmann, 1978)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Puberty is delayed in male winter hamsters compared to summer hamsters.
source: We confirmed that puberty is delayed in male winter hamsters compared to summer hamsters in the present experiment by measuring their gonadal weights across ages (Appendix 1 - Supplementary Analysis 5).
evidence: Supported by data in supplementary analysis.

claim: In male summer hamsters, dopamine input density to the prefrontal cortex increases during adolescence, after 15 days of age and before 80 days of age.
source: In male summer hamsters, dopamine input density to the prefrontal cortex increases during adolescence, after 15 days of age and before 80 days of age (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Prefrontal cortex dopamine innervation in male summer hamsters continues to increase after 80 days of age.
source: Prefrontal cortex dopamine innervation in summer hamsters continues to increase after 80 days of age (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In male winter hamsters, dopamine innervation to the prefrontal cortex is delayed until after 80 days.
source: In male winter hamsters, dopamine innervation to the prefrontal cortex is delayed until after 80 days, which coincides with their delayed pubertal onset (Figure 3D, Appendix 1 - Supplementary Analysis 5).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 3D and supplementary analysis.

claim: An environmental cue can determine the timing of adolescent brain development.
source: This demonstrates that an environmental cue can determine the timing of adolescent brain development.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the hamster photoperiod experiments.

claim: UNC5C expression in dopamine axons in the nucleus accumbens appears only after the onset of adolescence in male summer hamsters.
source: UNC5C expression was apparent only after the onset of adolescence in summer hamsters (Figure 3E, F, and G), as observed in male mice.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry images in Figures 3E, F, and G.

claim: UNC5C expression in dopamine axons in the nucleus accumbens is delayed in male winter hamsters, not appearing until after 80 days of age.
source: However, UNC5C expression was delayed in male winter hamsters – this group did not show UNC5C expression in dopamine axons in the nucleus accumbens until after 80 days of age (Figure 3H, I, and J).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry images in Figures 3H, I, and J.

claim: The delayed timing of UNC5C expression in male winter hamsters aligns with delayed mesocortical dopamine axon growth and pubertal onset.
source: This aligns with the delayed timing of mesocortical dopamine axon growth and pubertal onset in male winter hamsters and demonstrates that the emergence of UNC5C is a marker of adolescent onset in male mice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the parallel timing of UNC5C expression, dopamine innervation, and puberty.

claim: The emergence of UNC5C is a marker of adolescent onset in male hamsters.
source: This aligns with the delayed timing of mesocortical dopamine axon growth and pubertal onset in male winter hamsters and demonstrates that the emergence of UNC5C is a marker of adolescent onset in male mice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the correlation between UNC5C expression and adolescent developmental markers.

claim: Increased willingness to enter a novel environment is a behavioural characteristic of adolescence.
source: A behavioural characteristic of adolescence is increased willingness to enter a novel environment, a behaviour that assumes an increased amount of risk (Arrant et al., 2013; Lynn and Brown, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Time spent in the light compartment in the light/dark test is dopamine-dependent.
source: Time spent in the light compartment is dopamine-dependent (Bahi and Dreyer, 2019; Gao and Cutler, 1993)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Time spent in the light compartment in the light/dark test peaks in adolescence.
source: and peaks in adolescence (Arrant et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In male summer hamsters, risk taking increases across adolescence, peaks around 50 days, then subsequently declines.
source: In male summer hamsters, the risk taking increases across adolescence, peaks around 50 days, then subsequently declines (Figure 3K).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The adolescent increase in risk taking is protracted in male winter hamsters, showing a gradual, consistent increase rather than a peak and decline.
source: However, the adolescent increase in risk taking is protracted in winter hamsters: across the age range examined we observe a gradual, consistent increase in risk taking rather than a peak and decline.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: At 215 days of age, there is no difference in risk taking between male summer and winter hamsters.
source: In these hamsters, we find no difference in risk taking between the male summer and winter groups (Figure 3L)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: After 80 days, risk taking begins to decline in male winter hamsters and by 215 days it has declined to the same level as in summer hamsters.
source: demonstrating that, after 80 days, risk taking begins to decline in male winter hamsters and that by 215 days it has declined to the same level as in summer hamsters.
evidence: Inferred from the behavioral data at different ages.

claim: Male hamsters raised under summer-mimicking long days and winter-mimicking short days both ultimately make the transition to the adult behavioural phenotype.
source: Male hamsters raised under summer-mimicking long days and winter-mimicking short days both ultimately make the transition to the adult behavioural phenotype.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the behavioral data showing convergence at 215 days.

claim: Both male summer and winter hamsters show peaks in novel object exploration around 50 days old.
source: Both male summer and winter hamsters show peaks in novel object exploration around 50 days old, however the developmental shifts in behaviour around that peak are significantly more substantial in the summer males compared to the winter males (Appendix 1 - Supplementary Analysis 8).
evidence: Supported by data in supplementary analysis.

claim: Developmental shifts in novel object exploration around the peak are significantly more substantial in summer males compared to winter males.
source: Both male summer and winter hamsters show peaks in novel object exploration around 50 days old, however the developmental shifts in behaviour around that peak are significantly more substantial in the summer males compared to the winter males (Appendix 1 - Supplementary Analysis 8).
evidence: Supported by data in supplementary analysis.

claim: At 215 days of age, there is no difference in novel object exploration between male summer and winter hamsters.
source: In 215-day-old hamsters, there is no difference in novel object exploration between summer and winter males (Appendix 1 - Supplementary Analysis 9).
evidence: Supported by data in supplementary analysis.

claim: Under a summer-mimicking daylength, dopamine innervation to the medial prefrontal cortex increases between 15 and 80 days of age in female hamsters.
source: Under a summer-mimicking daylength, dopamine innervation to the medial prefrontal cortex increases between 15 and 80 days of age, similar to male summer hamsters (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There is no further increase in dopamine innervation density after 80 days of age in female summer hamsters.
source: There is no further increase in innervation density after 80 days of age, consistent with earlier adolescent development in females observed in other rodent species (Juraska and Willing, 2017; Kopec et al., 2018; Reynolds and Flores, 2021; Spear, 2000; Westbrook et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 4C and citations to previous literature.

claim: Puberty is delayed in female winter hamsters compared to summer hamsters.
source: We confirmed that puberty is delayed in female winter hamsters compared to summer hamsters by measuring their uterine weights (Appendix 1 - Supplementary Analysis 6) and vaginal opening (Appendix 1 - Supplementary Analysis 7) across ages.
evidence: Supported by data in supplementary analyses.

claim: When housed under a winter-mimicking daylength, dopamine input density in the prefrontal cortex of female hamsters reaches adult levels prior to 15 days of age.
source: When housed under a winter-mimicking daylength, dopamine input density in the prefrontal cortex of female hamsters is not delayed as in males, but rather reaches adult levels prior to 15 days of age (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The finding that dopamine innervation reaches adult levels prior to 15 days in female winter hamsters was replicated in a separate, independent cohort.
source: We replicated this unexpected finding in a separate, independent cohort of female winter hamsters (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Winter photoperiod shows an intervention that accelerates adolescent cortical development in female hamsters.
source: This surprising result shows an intervention that accelerates adolescent cortical development.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the accelerated dopamine innervation in female winter hamsters.

claim: Dopamine innervation increases between 10 and 15 days of age in female winter hamsters.
source: Dopamine innervation increases during this period (Figure 4F), well before normal adolescence and long before pubertal development.
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A key marker of adolescent neurodevelopment is accelerated and dissociated from puberty in female hamsters raised under winter-mimicking short days.
source: This is an extraordinary phenomenon: a key marker of adolescent neurodevelopment is accelerated and dissociated from puberty in female hamsters raised under winter-mimicking short days (Appendix 1 - Supplementary Analyses 6,7).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the timing of dopamine innervation relative to pubertal markers.

claim: The early increase in prefrontal cortex dopamine terminals in female winter hamsters is followed by a dramatic reduction between 80 and 215 days of age.
source: The early increase in prefrontal cortex dopamine terminals in winter females is followed by a dramatic reduction between 80 and 215 days of age (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification data shown in Figures 4D and E.

claim: The reduction in dopamine terminals between 80 and 215 days in female winter hamsters overlaps with the delayed timing of puberty in these females.
source: This overlaps with the delayed timing of puberty in these females (Butler et al., 2007; Appendix 1 - Supplementary Analyses 6,7).
evidence: Supported by comparison of dopamine innervation timing with pubertal markers and citation.

claim: Synaptic pruning in the cortex is a well-known component of adolescent neural development across species.
source: Synaptic pruning in the cortex is a well-known component of adolescent neural development across species (Huttenlocher, 1984; Koss et al., 2014; Petanjek et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Under normal conditions, the effect of pruning on dopamine synapses is likely masked by the growth of new dopamine axons to the prefrontal cortex.
source: Under normal conditions, the effect of pruning on dopamine synapses is likely masked by the growth of new dopamine axons to the prefrontal cortex (Manitt et al., 2013; Manitt et al., 2011; Reynolds et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In female winter hamsters, the growth of dopamine axons to the prefrontal cortex occurs early while synaptic pruning appears to occur later.
source: In the case of female winter hamsters, we hypothesise that the growth of dopamine axons to the prefrontal cortex occurs early while synaptic pruning, including dopamine synapses, appears to occur later.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the observed temporal pattern of dopamine innervation changes.

claim: Female winter hamsters show a dissociation between two cortical developmental processes that are normally simultaneous.
source: This leads to a remarkable dissociation between two cortical developmental processes that are normally simultaneous, the behavioural implications of which are unclear.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the temporal separation of dopamine axon growth and pruning.

claim: At 10 and 15 days of age, UNC5C expression is present only in female winter hamsters, not in summer hamsters.
source: At 10 and 15 days of age, UNC5C expression is present only in the winter hamsters (Figure 4G, H, K, and L)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry images in Figures 4G, H, K, and L.

claim: At 80 and 215 days of age, UNC5C expression is apparent in both female summer and winter hamsters.
source: but at 80 and 215 days of age, UNC5C expression is apparent in both summer and winter hamsters (Figure 4I, J, M, and N).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry images in Figures 4I, J, M, and N.

claim: In female summer and winter hamsters, the adolescent increase and peak in risk taking occurs between the ages of 15 and 80 days.
source: In female summer and winter hamsters, the adolescent increase and peak in risk taking occurs between the ages of 15 and 80 days, as it does in summer daylength males (Figure 4O).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4O.

claim: The peak in risk taking is delayed in female winter hamsters compared to summer females.
source: However, contrary to what we would expect, the peak in winter females is delayed compared to summer females.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4O.

claim: A delayed peak in novel object investigation is also observed for female winter hamsters.
source: A delayed peak is also observed for winter females in novel object investigation (Appendix 1 - Supplementary Analysis 10).
evidence: Supported by data in supplementary analysis.

claim: At 215 days of age, there is no difference in risk taking between female summer and winter hamsters.
source: When we assessed an independent cohort of 215-day-old female hamsters, we found no difference in risk taking (Figure 4P)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4P.

claim: At 215 days of age, there is no difference in novel object investigation between female summer and winter hamsters.
source: or novel object investigation (Appendix 1 - Supplementary Analysis 11) between groups
evidence: Supported by data in supplementary analysis.

claim: Female summer and winter hamsters both eventually reach the same adult level of risk taking.
source: indicating that, like males, female summer and winter hamsters both eventually reach the same adult level of risk taking.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the behavioral data at 215 days.

claim: In both sexes, hamsters housed under a summer-mimicking daylength showed an adolescent peak in risk taking at an age predicted based on results from other rodents.
source: In both sexes, hamsters housed under a summer-mimicking daylength showed an adolescent peak in risk taking at an age that we would predict based on results from other rodents (Arrant et al., 2013; Pietropaolo et al., 2004; Tanaka, 2015).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data and citations to previous literature.

claim: When raised under a winter-mimicking daylength, hamsters of either sex show a protracted peak in risk taking.
source: When raised under a winter-mimicking daylength, hamsters of either sex show a protracted peak in risk taking.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figures 3K and 4O.

claim: In males, the risk-taking peak is delayed beyond 80 days of age under winter photoperiod, but the delay is substantially less in females.
source: In males, it is delayed beyond 80 days of age, but the delay is substantially less in females.
evidence: Supported by comparison of behavioral data in Figures 3K and 4O.

claim: The timing of the risk-taking peak in female winter hamsters may reflect a balance between different adolescent developmental processes.
source: Our interpretation of this finding is that the timing of the risk-taking peak in females may reflect a balance between different adolescent developmental processes.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: The fact that dopamine axon growth is accelerated in female winter hamsters does not imply that all adolescent maturational processes are accelerated.
source: The fact that dopamine axon growth is accelerated does not imply that all adolescent maturational processes are accelerated.
evidence: Logical inference from the observation of dissociated developmental processes.

claim: Some adolescent maturational processes may be delayed in female winter hamsters, such as those that induce axon pruning in the cortex.
source: Some may be delayed, e.g., those that induce axon pruning in the cortex.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the observed pattern of dopamine innervation changes.

claim: The timing of the risk-taking peak in female winter hamsters may reflect the amalgamation of developmental processes that are advanced with those that are delayed.
source: The timing of the risk-taking peak in winter female hamsters may therefore reflect the amalgamation of developmental processes that are advanced with those that are delayed – producing a behavioural effect that is timed somewhere in the middle.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: Netrin-1 signalling provides the 'stay-or-go' 'decision making' conducted by dopamine axons that innervate the nucleus accumbens at the onset of adolescence.
source: Netrin-1 signalling provides the 'stay-or-go' 'decision making' conducted by dopamine axons that innervate the nucleus accumbens at the onset of adolescence (Cuesta et al., 2020; Reynolds et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: UNC5C expression by dopamine axons marks the timing at which the 'stay-or-go' decision is made.
source: UNC5C expression by these dopamine axons marks the timing at which this decision is made.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the correlation between UNC5C expression and dopamine axon growth timing.

claim: In mice, UNC5C expression coincides with sex differences in both adolescent and pubertal development.
source: In mice, UNC5C expression coincides with sex differences in both adolescent and pubertal development.
evidence: Supported by the observed earlier UNC5C expression in female mice.

claim: Females show earlier UNC5C expression in dopamine axons compared to males in mice.
source: Females, which develop earlier, show earlier UNC5C expression in dopamine axons compared to males.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2.

claim: Male hamsters raised under a winter-mimicking daylength delay not only puberty, but also adolescent dopamine and behavioural maturation.
source: As we show here, male hamsters raised under a winter-mimicking daylength delay not only puberty, but also adolescent dopamine and behavioural maturation.
evidence: Supported by data on dopamine innervation, UNC5C expression, and behavior in male winter hamsters.

claim: Female hamsters under winter photoperiod delay puberty but accelerate dopamine axon growth.
source: In contrast, female hamsters under identical conditions delay puberty but accelerate dopamine axon growth, a key marker of adolescent brain development.
evidence: Supported by data on pubertal markers and dopamine innervation in female winter hamsters.

claim: Behavioural shifts during adolescence appear to be delayed in female winter hamsters, but less substantially than in male hamsters.
source: Behavioural shifts during adolescence appear to be delayed in these females, but less substantially than in male hamsters.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data comparing male and female winter hamsters.

claim: Under all conditions, the developmental timing of UNC5C expression corresponds to the timing of dopamine innervation of the prefrontal cortex.
source: Notably, under all conditions, the developmental timing of UNC5C expression corresponds to the timing of dopamine innervation of the prefrontal cortex.
evidence: Supported by parallel observations across all experimental conditions in mice and hamsters.

claim: In both mice and hamsters, the emergence of UNC5C expression coincides with the onset of dopamine axon growth to the prefrontal cortex.
source: In both mice and hamsters, the emergence of UNC5C expression coincides with the onset of dopamine axon growth to the prefrontal cortex, a key characteristic of the adolescent transition period.
evidence: Supported by data across all experiments showing parallel timing.

claim: Netrin-1 signalling in the nucleus accumbens is responsible for coordinating whether dopamine axons grow in adolescence.
source: While previously we have shown that the Netrin-1 signalling in the nucleus accumbens is responsible for coordinating whether dopamine axons grow in adolescence (Reynolds and Flores, 2021; Cuesta et al., 2020; Reynolds et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Netrin-1 signalling is key to determining how and when dopamine axon growth occurs as a marker of adolescence.
source: here we propose that Netrin-1 signalling is also key to determining how and when this marker of adolescence occurs.
evidence: Proposed conclusion based on the findings in this manuscript.

claim: Nearly every dopamine varicosity in the prefrontal cortex forms a synapse.
source: TH-positive varicosities were used as the counting unit to obtain a measure of dopamine presynaptic density because nearly every dopamine varicosity in the prefrontal cortex forms a synapse (Séguéla et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Varicosities represent sites where neurotransmitter synthesis, packaging, release, and reuptake most often occur.
source: Varicosities also represent sites where neurotransmitter synthesis, packaging, release, and reuptake most often occur (Benes et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.
